chapter_title: Building a Simple Web Server with Flask
chapter_summary:
Flask is a lightweight Python web framework. It is perfect for Raspberry Pi projects because it is easy to learn, has few dependencies, and can serve a web interface from the Pi itself. With Flask, you can create a dashboard that controls LEDs, displays sensor readings, and triggers actions from any device on the network. Install Flask in a virtual environment: ```bash python3 -m venv web_env source web_env/bin/activate pip install flask gpiozero ``` A minimal Flask application looks like this: ```python from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route("/") def home(): return "Hello from Raspberry Pi!" if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True) ``` The `host="0.0.0.0"` setting makes the server accessible from other devices on the network, not just from the Pi itself. Save the script as `app.py` and run it with `python3 app.py`. Then open a browser and navigate to `http://raspberrypi.local:5000` or the Pi's IP address followed by `:5000`. To control an LED from the web, you can add more routes: ```python from flask import Flask from gpiozero import LED app = Flask(__name__) led = LED(17) @app.route("/") def index(): return """

Pi LED Control

""" @app.route("/on") def turn_on(): led.on() return "LED is ON. Back" @app.route("/off") def turn_off(): led.off() return "LED is OFF. Back" if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000) ``` This is simple but has a limitation: each button click navigates to a new page. A better approach uses POST requests and JavaScript, but for beginners, link-based control is a good starting point. To display sensor data, create a route that reads a sensor and returns formatted HTML: ```python from flask import Flask from gpiozero import MCP3008 app = Flask(__name__) adc = MCP3008(channel=0) @app.route("/") def index(): voltage = adc.value * 3.3 return f"

Sensor Reading

Voltage: {voltage:.2f} V

" if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000) ``` For production use, Flask's built-in server is not ideal. You can deploy with Gunicorn or run the app behind a reverse proxy with Nginx. For learning and local networks, the built-in server is fine.

screens.title: Building a Simple Web Server with Flask
screens.subtitle: Serve pages, handle routes, control GPIO, and show sensor data from your Pi

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how a lightweight Python framework called Flask turns your Raspberry Pi into a tiny web server. We will cover installing Flask inside a virtual environment, creating routes that return H T M L, and connecting those routes to physical hardware like an LED or an analog sensor. You will see a minimal working app, learn why the server needs to bind to all network interfaces on the Pi, and examine simple code that reads a sensor and returns a formatted value. This matters because building a web interface lets any device on the same Wi‑Fi network interact with your Pi without extra software. A concrete example you will follow is a three-button dashboard: turn an LED on, turn it off, and read a sensor value. Along the way we will highlight one common misconception — that the built‑in Flask server is production ready; it is fine for learning and local networks, but for outward‑facing deployment you will later use a production server and reverse proxy. By the end you should be able to run a basic Flask app on the Pi, test it from your phone, and extend it to control GPIO or show sensor readings.

keyIdea.text: Flask provides a minimal web layer on the Pi so browsers can control hardware and view sensors over your local network.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build and why they matter

narration.text: By the end of these exercises you will be able to install Flask in an isolated environment, write routes that return H T M L, drive a GPIO pin from a browser request, and read analog or digital sensor values and display them on a page. Installing inside a virtual environment keeps your system Python clean and avoids package conflicts. Writing routes teaches you the server idea: a URL maps to a small Python function that returns a response. Controlling GPIO from routes gives you a practical bridge between the network and physical hardware — for example, toggling an LED from your phone. Reading sensor data and formatting it on a route shows how to combine hardware input and web output so a dashboard can show real measurements. Each skill matters: installation ensures reproducible projects, routes form the app's structure, GPIO control unlocks physical interaction, and sensor display turns raw values into readable information. Expect to practice a simple LED control page and a sensor-read route that prints the voltage; these concrete exercises make the objectives tangible and testable.

keyIdea.text: Install and create basic routes so your Pi can serve pages and respond to browser requests.

Learning Objectives

Four core competencies you will verify through practice.

Install Flask in a virtualenv
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Mnemonic: isolated box
02
Create routes and serve HTML
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Write URL routes that map to functions returning HTML or text. This is how you build pages like a dashboard or sensor readout. Practice with a minimal "Hello" route first to confirm connectivity.

Mnemonic: URL → function → view
03
Control GPIO from a browser
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Use gpiozero inside route functions to toggle outputs like an LED when a route is visited. This connects the network to physical outputs and helps you prototype interactive projects quickly.

Mnemonic: click → request → action
04
Read and display sensor data

Read analog or digital sensors using gpiozero or an ADC and return the measurement as formatted HTML so a phone or browser sees live values. This is essential for dashboards and monitoring.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Testing
screens.subtitle: How you'll check that each skill works

narration.text: Practical verification is part of each objective. After installing Flask you will run a minimal app that returns a short message, confirming the server starts without errors. For routes and H T M L, you will create a simple index route that returns an H T M L heading and then open that URL from another device on the same Wi‑Fi. To verify GPIO control you will wire an LED to the correct pin, run the route that sets the pin high, and observe the LED toggle. For sensors you will read a simple analog value and present it as a numeric voltage so you can see live changes. Each test is explicit: run the server, access the URL, observe the hardware or value, and stop the server. These checks teach debugging routines and build confidence. A common pitfall is forgetting to activate the virtual environment before installing packages, so verify environment activation as part of the install check. These practical checks make the objectives measurable and repeatable.

Concrete tests that prove each objective works on your Pi.

screens.title: What is Flask and why use it on a Pi?
screens.subtitle: A minimal web framework for building simple web interfaces and APIs

narration.text: Flask is a lightweight Python web framework that gives you a minimal, flexible way to turn functions into web endpoints. On a Raspberry Pi it is a practical choice because it has few dependencies, is easy to learn, and serves pages directly from the device. A Flask app is just a Python script that creates an app object and maps URL routes to functions which return text or H T M L. For example, a function can return a heading or a formatted sensor value. A concrete example you will use is a tiny app that returns the text hello from Raspberry Pi when the root URL is visited. That shows the full path: browser makes an HTTP request, Flask receives it, the mapped function runs, and a response is returned. A common misconception is that a framework must be heavy to be useful. Flask demonstrates the opposite: a small tool can provide the essential structure for interaction without hiding how requests map to code. Key practical points are: keep the app simple for learning, run it locally for testing, and use it to prototype dashboards and hardware control before moving to more complex deployment setups. How could you use this same pattern to make a temperature readout available to your phone?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Flask maps URLs to Python functions so a browser can trigger code or receive information from your Pi.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is Flask and why use it on a Pi?

Flask is a tiny, explicit web layer

It exposes Python functions as web endpoints so browsers can trigger actions or receive data.

Minimal app example
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/")
def home():
    return "Hello from Raspberry Pi!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)
Bulleted explanation:
  • Create an app object and use a decorator to map a route.
  • The function returns the response the browser displays.
  • Binding to 0.0.0.0 makes the server reachable from other devices on the network.
Concrete example & analogy
Imagine the Pi as a small shop and Flask as the shopkeeper. A browser is a customer asking for a product. A route is a labeled shelf; when the customer looks there, the shopkeeper brings back a specific item or triggers an action like flipping a switch. This helps you reason about requests and responses when you connect hardware like an LED.
Key takeaway
Flask is intentionally small: learn request→handler→response to control hardware from the network.
Common mistake
Treating Flask's built‑in server as production. For learning it's fine; for public services use a production server later.

screens.title: Set up a virtual environment and install dependencies
screens.subtitle: Create an isolated environment, activate it, and install Flask and gpiozero

narration.text: Creating a virtual environment is a small upfront step that pays off by keeping project packages isolated from the system Python. The steps are simple: first create the environment, then activate it in your shell, and finally install Flask and gpiozero. On the Pi you will run Python three -m venv web_env to make a folder that contains the isolated interpreter. Then source web_env/bin/activate enables the environment for the session. Once active, pip install flask gpiozero installs the packages only inside that environment. A concrete example: if you later install a different project that requires another version of Flask, each project can have its own environment without conflicts. People often forget to activate the virtual environment before installing packages or running the app; if that happens, packages may be installed globally and cause version issues. After installation, run python -c "import flask" as a quick smoke test to confirm the package is accessible. This process makes your development reproducible and easier to debug when dependencies change. Set up a virtual environment and install dependencies means use a virtual environment to install flask and gpiozero so project dependencies remain isolated and reproducible.. In practical terms, create an isolated environment, activate it, and install flask and gpiozero. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Install process
keyIdea.text: Use a virtual environment to install Flask and gpiozero so project dependencies remain isolated and reproducible.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Set up a virtual environment

Install steps

Three simple commands to prepare your Pi for Flask-based projects.

1. Create the environment
python3 -m venv web_env
This makes an isolated Python environment inside a folder named web_env.
2. Activate the environment
source web_env/bin/activate
Activating ensures subsequent installs go into web_env and that python points to the environment interpreter.
3. Install packages
pip install flask gpiozero
Install Flask for the web layer and gpiozero for GPIO access from Python.
Why this matters

Keeping dependencies isolated prevents version clashes between projects, makes deployment easier, and helps you debug missing-package errors quickly. It also makes it safe to experiment on the Pi without risking system packages.

Tip
If pip reports permissions or system-site packages, ensure the environment is activated and re-run the install inside it.
Common mistake
Forgetting to activate the virtualenv before running the app will lead to import failures or unexpected package versions.
Check your install
Quick test: python -c "import flask; print(flask.__version__)" to confirm Flask is available in the environment.

screens.title: Making the server reachable: host and port
screens.subtitle: Bind to 0.0.0.0 and test on port 5000 from another device

narration.text: When you run a Flask app on the Pi, the host and port settings determine who can reach it. By default, Flask binds to the local loopback interface, which only accepts requests from the Pi itself. Setting host to 0.0.0.0 tells Flask to listen on all network interfaces, allowing other devices on the same Wi‑Fi to connect. Using port 5000 is conventional for development; the URL you visit from another device looks like the Pi's IP followed by a colon and the port number. A concrete scenario: you run the app with host set to 0.0.0.0 and port 5000, then open http://raspberrypi. local:5000 or http://192.168.1.12:5000 on your phone to see the response. A common misunderstanding is thinking this exposes the Pi to the whole internet — it only makes it reachable on the local network unless you have forwarded ports or configured public access. For learning and local control, this is exactly what you want so you can test dashboards from any device on the same Wi‑Fi. Always stop the server when you're done and consider production servers and reverse proxies for wider deployment.

keyIdea.title: Networking
keyIdea.text: host="0.0.0.0" makes your Flask app accessible from other devices on the same network; port 5000 is the common development port.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Making the server reachable

Host and port explained

Use host and port to control who can connect and where the app listens.

Typical run command
app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
  • host="0.0.0.0" listens on all interfaces so other devices on the same network can connect.
  • port=5000 is the conventional development port; if occupied, choose another unused port.
  • To reach the server, use the Pi’s IP address or a local host name followed by the port.
Concrete example
Start the app on the Pi, find its IP using a network tool or the Pi’s settings, then open the IP with :5000 on your phone’s browser. You should see the app’s response if both devices are on the same Wi‑Fi.
Tip
If you cannot connect, verify the Pi and phone are on the same subnet and that no firewall is blocking traffic.
Misconception
Binding to 0.0.0.0 does not automatically expose your Pi to the internet; it only accepts local network connections unless additional routing is configured.
Check your URL
Use http://raspberrypi.local:5000 or http://PI_IP:5000 to connect from another device.

screens.title: Serve HTML pages and handle routes
screens.subtitle: Map URLs to functions that return HTML, text, or sensor data

narration.text: Routes are the core building blocks of a Flask app. A route decorator tells Flask which function should handle a given URL. The function can return plain text, an H T M L string, or render a template to produce richer pages. A concrete beginner example is an index route that returns an H T M L string with a heading and simple controls. For clarity, we will show the code as a static example so you can copy it into app dot P Y file. When the browser requests the root URL, Flask calls the function and returns whatever string it provides. A common beginner pitfall is embedding large H T M L blocks directly and making maintenance harder; templates separate H T M L from code and are a good next step. For now, the simple inline responses are useful to confirm connectivity and to prototype hardware triggers quickly. After you test a simple text response, replace it with formatted H T M L and later move it into a template folder. What route would you create to return the current sensor value as a labeled number?

keyIdea.title: Routes & responses
keyIdea.text: Use decorators to map URLs to Python functions that return text or HTML, forming pages and simple dashboards.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Serve HTML pages and handle routes

Route example

A minimal route that returns an HTML heading and links for testing.

Example code (static display)
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/")
def index():
    return "<h1>Pi LED Control</h1><p>Use your browser to send requests to control hardware.</p>"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
Note: angle brackets are escaped here for safe display. Copy the structure into your app file and test by visiting the Pi’s address from another device.
Explanation bullets
  • The @app.route decorator registers the URL route with Flask.
  • The index function returns a string that Flask sends as the HTTP response.
  • Start small with text responses, then move to templates for more complex HTML.
Try this
Create a second route named /status that returns a short status message you can check from your phone.

screens.title: Controlling an LED from the web
screens.subtitle: Simple route-based control vs. POST/JS for smoother UX

narration.text: Controlling an LED from a browser is a classic Pi web project. One very simple approach uses separate routes for on and off: visiting /on calls a function that turns the LED on and returns a confirmation page, while /off turns it off. This route-based method is easy for beginners and demonstrates the request→action relationship clearly. A limitation is that each click navigates to a new page, which can feel clunky. An alternative is to use a POST request or JavaScript to call the server asynchronously and update the page without navigation; this gives a smoother user experience but adds complexity. A concrete example: with gpiozero you create led = LED(17) at module scope, then in route functions call led. on() or led. off(). A common misconception is that web control must be immediate and real-time; for many projects the simple page refresh model is perfectly adequate. Later, when you need non‑blocking updates or richer UI, add JavaScript that sends fetch requests to POST endpoints and updates the DOM without leaving the page. Which approach fits your project depends on how polished you want the dashboard to be versus how much code you want to write.

keyIdea.title: Control methods
keyIdea.text: Begin with route-based GET triggers to control GPIO, and move to POST or JavaScript calls for a smoother, interactive interface.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Controlling an LED from the web

Two practical methods

Compare a simple route-based approach with a JavaScript-enhanced approach for user experience.

Route-based (beginner)
from gpiozero import LED
led = LED(17)

@app.route('/on')
def turn_on():
    led.on()
    return 'LED is ON'
Simple to implement and great for testing hardware control. Each action is triggered by a GET request and returns a small response.
POST / JS (smoother UX)
Use a POST endpoint and client‑side JavaScript to call it asynchronously and update the page state without navigation. This requires extra code but creates a more responsive dashboard.
When to use
Choose POST/JS when you need immediate UI updates or when multiple controls are active simultaneously.
Concrete example
Wire LED to pin 17, test route-based on/off behavior, then decide whether to upgrade UI with JavaScript.
Safety note
Always include a resistor with an LED and confirm the correct pin numbering to avoid damaging hardware.
Check your understanding
Which method would you pick for a quick prototype you control only from your phone on the local network?

screens.title: Read sensor data and show it on a page
screens.subtitle: Use an ADC or gpiozero sensor object and return formatted HTML

narration.text: Displaying sensor data in a web page demonstrates how your Pi can bridge the physical and the networked world. Use an ADC like the MCP3008 for analog inputs or a gpiozero sensor object for digital sensors. The pattern is the same: create the sensor object at module scope, read its value in a route function, format the reading, and return it as H T M L. For example, reading an ADC channel value and converting it to voltage produces a concise H T M L response that you can check from any browser. A concrete snippet reads adc. value multiplied by 3.3 to get voltage and returns it inside a small H T M L paragraph. A common misconception is expecting live streaming; a simple route reads the value at request time — refresh the page to get a new reading. If you need continuous updates, combine the route with client-side polling or websockets later. For learning, the request-time read model is reliable and simple. After confirming a working readout, test small environmental changes to the sensor to see the reported value change.

keyIdea.title: Sensors
keyIdea.text: Read the sensor when a route is requested and return the value as formatted HTML; refresh or poll for updates.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Read sensor data and show it on a page

Sensor read route

Read an ADC channel and return a formatted voltage string to the browser.

Example ADC code
from flask import Flask
from gpiozero import MCP3008

app = Flask(__name__)
adc = MCP3008(channel=0)

@app.route('/')
def index():
    voltage = adc.value * 3.3
    return f"<h1>Sensor Reading</h1><p>Voltage: {voltage:.2f} V</p>"
This code reads the ADC at request time and returns a simple HTML fragment showing the voltage with two decimals.
Explanation bullets
  • adc.value returns a normalized number between 0 and 1 for MCP3008; multiply by reference voltage to get voltage.
  • Formatting with two decimals makes the readout easy to scan on a phone.
  • Request-time reads are simple to implement and reliable for manual refresh polling.
Try this
Wire an LDR or potentiometer to the ADC channel, then change the light or knob and refresh the page to observe the voltage change.

screens.title: Dashboard layout: simple HTML for controls and readouts
screens.subtitle: Design a clear page with labeled controls and sensor readouts for easy testing

narration.text: Designing a useful dashboard for your Pi is more about clear layout than fancy code. A simple page with a heading, separate labeled buttons for controls, and a sensor readout area gives you everything you need to test interactions from a phone. In the beginning keep H T M L inline for speed: an index route returns a small H T M L block with headings and descriptive text. Use labels to make it obvious what each control does and include a small status text that confirms actions. A concrete example is an index page with a heading Pi LED Control, two call-to-action links that map to on and off routes, and a sensor paragraph that shows the latest voltage. Remember to escape H T M L when displaying code in teaching materials; in your app file use real tags so the browser renders the interface. A common mistake is overcrowding the page with too many controls; start with three items: Turn On LED, Turn Off LED, and Read Sensor. This keeps testing focused and reduces accidental interactions. Once working, you can refactor the H T M L into templates for maintainability.

keyIdea.title: Simple dashboard
keyIdea.text: A clean, labeled HTML page with a few controls and a readout area makes testing and prototyping straightforward.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Dashboard layout

Design a clear page for controls and readings

Start with a single page that groups controls and sensor output to make testing simple.

Example HTML layout (concept)
<h1>Pi LED Control</h1>
<div>Turn the LED on or off:</div>
<div><a href="/on">On</a> <a href="/off">Off</a></div>
<div id="sensor">Voltage: -- V</div>
Start with simple anchors for testing, then replace them with JavaScript calls for a smoother interface once the backend works.
Practical guidance
  • Group related controls and label them clearly to avoid accidental activation.
  • Include a small status text that confirms the last action or shows the latest sensor reading.
  • Keep the initial UI minimal: three controls are enough to validate the core interaction loop.
Key takeaway
A clean dashboard makes debugging faster and testing from a phone simpler.

screens.title: Production considerations and next steps
screens.subtitle: When to use Gunicorn or Nginx and when Flask's server is sufficient

narration.text: Flask's built‑in development server is simple and convenient for learning and local network projects, but it is not optimized for production. The chapter notes two common next steps: running the app with Gunicorn or placing the app behind a reverse proxy like Nginx. Gunicorn is a production-ready WSGI server that can manage multiple worker processes and improve robustness. Nginx can act as a reverse proxy to serve static assets, handle TLS, and forward requests to your application server. For local testing and phone-based control on the same Wi‑Fi, the built‑in server is entirely adequate and faster to set up. A concrete rule of thumb: while experimenting or in small home networks, keep using Flask's server; if you plan to expose the Pi to external traffic, move to a production server and configure a reverse proxy. A common misconception is thinking these steps are required for every project — they are necessary only when reliability, performance, or public access is required. The next practical steps are to consolidate your H T M L into templates, secure the Pi, and learn basic Gunicorn/Nginx deployment when you are ready.

keyIdea.title: Deployment
keyIdea.text: Use Flask's server for learning and local testing; choose Gunicorn and a reverse proxy for production or public exposure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Production considerations and next steps

When to move beyond the built-in server

The built-in server is great for learning; Gunicorn and Nginx help when you need production features.

Development server
Flask's server is simple to run and ideal for experiments and local dashboards. It is not designed for handling heavy load or public internet exposure.
Production options
  • Gunicorn: a WSGI server that runs multiple worker processes for improved stability.
  • Nginx: a reverse proxy to serve static files, terminate TLS, and forward requests to Gunicorn.
Practical next steps
After you complete the hands‑on activity, refactor your HTML into templates, add simple client-side code if you want a smoother UI, and later explore Gunicorn/Nginx when you want to host beyond your local network.
Misconception check
You do not need production servers for local learning; only adopt them when availability, performance, or public access is required.

screens.title: What to Remember — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's consolidate the most important concepts. First, Flask is a minimal web framework that maps URLs to Python functions; this lets you turn simple code into web-accessible behaviors. Second, routes and views form the structure of your app: each route decorator registers a function that returns text or H T M L, which the browser then displays. Third, controlling GPIO from a web request connects network inputs to hardware outputs; a route can call gpiozero functions to toggle an LED or perform other actions. Each of these ideas is a small building block — combine them to create dashboards, control panels, or sensor readouts accessible from any device on your local network. Think about which idea you would apply first on your Pi to make a small functional demo. What to Remember — Part 1 means flask + routes + gpio give you a simple pattern to build interactive pi projects accessible from a browser.. In practical terms, three essential ideas from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Core reminders
keyIdea.text: Flask + routes + GPIO give you a simple pattern to build interactive Pi projects accessible from a browser.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts — Part 1

Key Concepts

Three compact reminders to keep handy while you work.

Flask framework
A lightweight layer that exposes Python functions over HTTP for easy prototyping.
Routes & views
Decorators map URLs to functions that return HTML or text responses.
GPIO control
Use gpiozero calls inside route functions to control LEDs or other outputs from the web.
Summary takeaway

Combine Flask routes with gpiozero reads or writes to create accessible, hands-on Pi projects on your local network.

screens.title: What to Remember — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders and next steps

narration.text: A few final practical reminders: first, always use a virtual environment for each project so dependencies stay isolated and reproducible. Second, test your app on the local network by binding the server to 0.0.0.0 and visiting the Pi’s IP with the port number to confirm accessibility from another device. Third, balance simplicity and usability: route-based GET controls are excellent for quick prototypes, while POST or JavaScript calls can create smoother dashboards when you need them. As a next step, practice the hands-on activity: implement a three-button app to turn an LED on and off and read a sensor. That exercise ties together installation, routes, GPIO control, and sensor reading into a single, testable project and will solidify the concepts covered here. What to Remember — Part 2 means use virtualenv, bind to 0.0.0.0 for testing across devices, and choose route vs. js approaches based on your ux needs.. In practical terms, three practical reminders and next steps. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical next steps
keyIdea.text: Use virtualenv, bind to 0.0.0.0 for testing across devices, and choose route vs. JS approaches based on your UX needs.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts — Part 2

Practical reminders

Three actionable items to guide your next practice session.

Virtual environments
Isolate project packages to avoid version conflicts and to make development reproducible.
Network testing
Bind to 0.0.0.0 and use the Pi’s IP and port to confirm access from other devices on your Wi‑Fi.
Interaction choices
Use simple GET route triggers for prototypes; add POST/JS when you need a responsive UI.
Final task

Build the three-button Flask app: turn LED on, turn LED off, and read sensor. Test it from your phone to confirm end-to-end behavior.
